lessons.title: Workbook architecture
lessons.summary: Inputs, calculations and outputs, colour conventions and documentation.

steps.title: Design the flow before typing formulas
steps.body:
A clear workbook flows in one direction: inputs (assumptions, each entered once) → calculations (formulas only) → outputs (summaries, charts, checks).

Common conventions: blue for typed inputs, black for formulas, green for links to other sheets. Label units ($, %, rooms) and note the source of every input.
steps.deeper: Other professional standards: one row = one line item with the same formula across all periods; time runs left to right; no hard-coded numbers inside formulas; totals are calculated, never typed; a checks area shows whether the model reconciles. These habits make models easier to review and much harder to break.

steps.title: A well-structured block
steps.body: The fictional Harbour Crest model starts with clearly labelled inputs.
steps.note: Source note on B1: 'Property fact sheet, fictional.'

steps.title: Replace a hard-coded total
steps.prompt: B3 should hold available room nights. Write a formula that links to the inputs instead of typing 5,580.
hints: Available room nights = rooms x days.
steps.solution: =B1*B2. The model now updates when the room count or month length changes.

steps.question: A colleague typed 5580 into B3. Next month the hotel adds 20 rooms (B1 = 200). What does B3 show?
steps.reveal: A typed number never updates. The model now overstates occupancy because its denominator is too small.

steps.title: Linked versus typed
steps.prompt: Change the inputs and compare the linked formula with the typed value.
steps.observe: Set the month to 28 days: the typed value overstates capacity by 540 room nights.

steps.title: Structure prevents errors
steps.body: When every input is entered once and everything else is calculated, a change propagates everywhere automatically. Reviewers can test the model by changing inputs and watching outputs.
steps.misconception: 'I will remember to update it' does not scale. Hidden constants are the most common cause of model errors.

steps.title: Choose the better layout
steps.scenario: You are building a monthly forecast for the hotel.
steps.question: Which layout is best practice?
options: Assumptions typed inside each formula, e.g. =180*31*0.72
Inputs in a labelled assumptions block, calculations referencing them, outputs summarised separately
One sheet per month with values copied and pasted
Totals typed in by hand after checking with a calculator
steps.explanation: Separate, labelled inputs with linked calculations are transparent, consistent and easy to update.

questions.question: In common modeling convention, what does blue text usually indicate?
questions.explanation: Blue marks hard-coded inputs so reviewers know what can be changed.

questions.question: Which is a sign of good formula consistency?
options: Each month uses a slightly different formula
The same formula is used across every period in a row
questions.explanation: One row, one formula: if January's logic is right, all months are right.

points: Inputs → calculations → outputs.
Enter each assumption once; label units and sources.
One consistent formula per row; no typed totals.
Include checks that show the model reconciles.

lessons.title: Relative and absolute references
lessons.summary: Write one formula and copy it across twelve months correctly.

steps.title: References move when copied
steps.body:
A relative reference like B3 moves when you copy the formula: copied one column right, it becomes C3. An absolute reference like $B$1 stays fixed. Mixed references fix only the column ($B1) or only the row (B$1).

Use absolute references for single assumptions that every period uses, such as the room count.
steps.deeper: In Excel, press F4 while the cursor is on a reference to cycle through B1 → $B$1 → B$1 → $B1. When copying across columns, only the column part matters; when copying down rows, only the row part matters. FinPilot's Lab has a 'Fill right' command that copies a formula across a row the same way Excel does.

steps.title: Copying across months
steps.body: Room count in B1 (180); days per month in row 3.
steps.note: The first version silently multiplies by a blank cell.

steps.title: Write once, fill right
steps.prompt: In B4, write a formula for available room nights (rooms in B1 x days in row 3) that still works when FinPilot copies it to C4:E4.
hints: Which reference must stay pointing at B1 when copied right?
Anchor the room count with $ signs; leave the days reference relative.
steps.solution: =$B$1*B3. $B$1 stays fixed; B3 moves to C3, D3, E3.

steps.question: The formula =B$1*B3 in B4 is copied one column right to C4. What does it become?
steps.reveal: B$1 fixes only the row. Copied right, the column moves: C$1. Only $B$1 or $B1 keep pointing at column B.

steps.title: An anchored growth rate
steps.prompt: Monthly revenue grows from a base at a growth rate stored in one cell. Each month's formula refers to the anchored rate.
steps.observe: Change the single growth cell: every month updates, because each copy points at the same anchored cell.

steps.title: Anchor assumptions, let time move
steps.body: Inside a time series, references to the period (days, occupancy for that month) should be relative so they move with the column. References to single assumptions (room count, tax rate) should be absolute.
steps.misconception: Getting January right is not enough. Always check the last column too: errors from unanchored references often appear only in later periods.

steps.title: Predict the copy
steps.scenario: Cell C7 contains =$B$2*C5. You copy it to E9.
steps.question: What formula ends up in E9?
steps.explanation: $B$2 never moves. C5 moves 2 columns right and 2 rows down: E7.

questions.question: Which reference stays fixed when copied in any direction?
questions.explanation: Both column and row are anchored.

questions.question: You copy a formula across columns only. Which reference to the room count in B1 would also work?
questions.explanation: Copying across changes only the column, so fixing the column ($B) is sufficient.

points: Relative references move when copied; absolute ($B$1) do not.
Anchor single assumptions; keep period references relative.
Check the last period, not just the first.

lessons.title: SUM, IF and IFERROR
lessons.summary: Totals, decisions and handling errors without hiding mistakes.

steps.title: Three everyday functions
steps.body:
SUM(range) adds a range: =SUM(B2:M2).
IF(test, value_if_true, value_if_false) chooses between two results, e.g. =IF(B1>=B2,"Met","Missed").
IFERROR(value, fallback) replaces any error with a fallback.
steps.deeper: IFERROR is convenient but dangerous: it also hides typos, broken links and missing data. Prefer testing the specific condition you expect, for example =IF(B2=0,NA(),B1/B2) for a ratio whose denominator can be zero. NA() deliberately shows #N/A, which is honest: 'not available', not 'zero'.

steps.title: Examples
steps.note: An ADR of $0 suggests rooms were given away; #N/A says no rooms were sold.

steps.title: A target bonus with IF
steps.prompt: In B4, return the bonus in B3 if occupancy (B1) is at or above target (B2), otherwise 0.
steps.solution: =IF(B1>=B2,B3,0). Note >= so exactly hitting the target earns the bonus.

steps.question: B6 holds room revenue and B7 rooms sold. B7 is blank because the data has not arrived. What does =IFERROR(B6/B7,0) show?
steps.reveal: IFERROR turns the divide-by-zero error into 0, so missing data looks like a real ADR of $0.

steps.title: Honest versus hidden errors
steps.prompt: Set rooms sold to 0 and compare the two approaches.
steps.observe: With 0 rooms sold, the IF version shows #N/A (honest); the IFERROR version shows $0.00 (misleading).

steps.title: Handle the case you expect, expose the rest
steps.body: Use IF to handle a specific, expected situation such as a zero denominator. Leave unexpected errors visible so they get fixed.
steps.misconception: Wrapping everything in IFERROR makes a model look clean while it hides real problems.

steps.title: Pick the robust formula
steps.scenario: You need ADR (B1 = room revenue, B2 = rooms sold). Some future months have no data yet.
steps.question: Which formula is best?
explanations: Shows #DIV/0!, which is accurate but unexplained.
A blank hides every error, including typos.
steps.explanation: Test the expected condition and mark it as not available.

questions.question: =SUM(B1:B3) where B1 = 1,200,000, B2 = 1,100,000 and B3 contains the text 'n/a'. Result?

mistakes.message: SUM skips text inside a range rather than failing.

questions.question: Why is IFERROR risky in financial models?
options: It hides every error, including real mistakes
It is not available in Excel
questions.explanation: Errors are signals. IFERROR silences all of them.

points: SUM adds ranges and skips text.
IF chooses between results; use >= and <= carefully at thresholds.
Prefer IF(denominator=0,NA(),...) to IFERROR for expected cases.

lessons.title: Lookups and conditional sums
lessons.summary: XLOOKUP, INDEX/MATCH and SUMIFS for segment data.

steps.title: Find and add the right rows
steps.body:
XLOOKUP(value, lookup_range, return_range) finds a value and returns the matching item: the rate for a segment, the budget for a month.
INDEX(range, MATCH(value, lookup_range, 0)) does the same and works in every Excel version.
SUMIFS(sum_range, criteria_range, criterion, ...) adds only the rows that meet conditions, e.g. all Corporate room revenue.
steps.deeper: Always use exact matching for names and codes: MATCH(...,0), XLOOKUP's default, or VLOOKUP with FALSE as the last argument. VLOOKUP's default is approximate match, which can silently return the wrong row if the table is not sorted. When a value is not found, lookups return #N/A; that is useful, because it tells you a code is missing or misspelt.

steps.title: Segment rate table (fictional)
steps.body: Rates by market segment for one night.

steps.title: Look up the segment rate
steps.prompt: In E1, return the rate for the segment named in D1, using the table in A1:B4. XLOOKUP or INDEX/MATCH are both fine.
hints: Look up D1 in the names (A1:A4) and return from the rates (B1:B4).

steps.question: D1 is changed to 'Crew', which is not in the table. What does an exact-match lookup return?
options: The first rate in the list
steps.reveal: #N/A means not found. That is the right signal: the segment is missing from the table.

steps.title: Segment mix and blended rate
steps.prompt: Lookups feed segment rates into revenue. Change the mix and watch the blended ADR.
steps.observe: Shift 800 rooms from Leisure to Group: total rooms are unchanged but blended ADR falls. That is a mix effect.

steps.title: Lookups make models data-driven
steps.body: Lookups let one formula pull the right number for any segment or month, so the model scales without manual edits. SUMIFS turns transaction lists into summaries.
steps.misconception: VLOOKUP without FALSE uses approximate matching and can return a wrong rate without any error.

steps.title: Sum corporate revenue
steps.question: Bookings are listed in A2:A7 (segment) and C2:C7 (revenue). In F1, sum the revenue for the segment named in E1 with SUMIFS.

questions.question: In SUMIFS, which argument comes first?
What does MATCH("Group",A1:A4,0) return for the table above?
questions.explanation: MATCH returns the position; INDEX then fetches the value at that position.

points: XLOOKUP / INDEX-MATCH return a matching value; use exact match.
#N/A from a lookup means 'not found' - investigate it.
SUMIFS summarises lists by one or more conditions.

lessons.title: Dates and monthly time series
lessons.summary: Month lengths, EOMONTH and building a monthly timeline.

steps.title: Dates are numbers
steps.body:
Spreadsheets store dates as serial numbers (days since 1900), so you can do arithmetic with them. Useful functions: DATE(y,m,d) builds a date, EOMONTH(date, n) returns the last day of the month n months away, DAY(date) returns the day number.

Days in a month: =DAY(EOMONTH(date,0)).
steps.deeper: Monthly models usually have a header row of month-end dates: the first is typed (or built with DATE) and each next one is =EOMONTH(previous,1). Days in each month then come from those dates, so leap years are handled automatically. Hotels care because available room nights depend on month length: February has about 10% fewer nights than January.

steps.title: Days drive capacity
steps.body: For a 180-room hotel in 2026 (not a leap year).
steps.note: Hard-coding 30 days for every month misstates capacity by up to 7%.

steps.title: Days in the month
steps.prompt: B1 holds a date. In B2, return the number of days in that month using EOMONTH and DAY.
hints: EOMONTH(B1,0) gives the last day of B1's month.
DAY() of that date is the number of days.

steps.question: How many days does =DAY(EOMONTH(DATE(2028,2,1),0)) return?
steps.reveal: 2028 is a leap year, so February has 29 days.

steps.title: Let dates drive the timeline
steps.body: When month lengths come from dates, the model stays right if the start year changes, and every period-based calculation (capacity, payroll days, interest) is consistent.
steps.misconception: Averaging monthly percentages ignores different month lengths. Time-weighted results come from totals.

steps.title: Quarterly capacity
steps.scenario: A 220-room hotel is forecasting the first quarter of 2026 (January to March).
steps.question: How many available room nights are there in Q1 2026?

mistakes.message: 2026 is not a leap year: February has 28 days, so Q1 has 90 days.

questions.question: Which formula gives the last day of the month after the date in A1?
questions.explanation: EOMONTH(A1,1) moves one month ahead and returns its last day.

questions.question: Why derive days in month from dates rather than typing them?
options: It handles leap years and changes of start date automatically
questions.explanation: Derived values cannot drift out of sync with the timeline.

points: Dates are serial numbers you can calculate with.
Days in month = DAY(EOMONTH(date,0)).
Build the month header with EOMONTH(previous,1).

lessons.title: Formula auditing and error prevention
lessons.summary: Read error values, trace links and build checks.

steps.title: Four kinds of problems
steps.body:
Formula errors: the formula is broken (#NAME?, #REF!, circular reference).
Invalid inputs: wrong type or impossible value (text in a number cell, occupancy of 120%).
Missing data: a needed value is blank or not found (#N/A).
Unreasonable results: the maths works but the answer makes no business sense (an ADR of $12 for a luxury hotel).
steps.deeper: Audit techniques: trace precedents (what a cell uses) and dependents (what uses it); check formula consistency across a row; build check cells that return TRUE/FALSE (balance sheet balances, totals match, rooms sold ≤ available); review extreme inputs (zero, very large, negative). Never force a check to pass with an unexplained 'plug' number.

steps.title: Error values and what they mean
steps.body: FinPilot uses Excel's error codes plus two of its own.

rows: Lookup not found / data not available
A real Excel feature FinPilot does not support yet

steps.note: In the Lab, select any cell and choose 'Explain' to see its precedents, dependents and error source.

steps.title: Build a balance check
steps.prompt: In B4, write a check that returns TRUE when assets (B1) equal liabilities (B2) plus equity (B3) within $0.01, and FALSE otherwise.
hints: The difference assets - liabilities - equity should be (almost) zero.
ABS() removes the sign; compare with a small tolerance.
steps.solution: =ABS(B1-B2-B3)<0.01. A tolerance avoids false alarms from tiny rounding differences.

steps.question: A model divides room revenue by rooms sold, and rooms sold for December is still blank. What appears?
steps.reveal: A blank counts as zero in arithmetic, so the division fails with #DIV/0!.

steps.title: Valid maths, unreasonable answer
steps.prompt: Push rooms sold above capacity. The arithmetic still works, so a check must catch it.
steps.observe: At 6,000 rooms sold occupancy shows 107.5%: mathematically valid, physically impossible. The check flags it.

steps.title: Checks catch what errors cannot
steps.body: Spreadsheets only raise errors for broken maths. Business impossibilities need explicit checks, and a model's checks should all pass before anyone relies on it.
steps.misconception: 'No error values' does not mean 'correct'. A model can be error-free and wrong.

steps.title: Spot the inconsistent formula
steps.scenario: Row 16 (rooms sold) contains: B16 =B15*B10, C16 =C15*C10, D16 =D15*C10, E16 =E15*E10.
steps.question: Which cell is wrong?
steps.explanation: D16 uses February's occupancy (C10) instead of March's (D10). Inconsistent formulas in a row are a classic error, often caused by manual edits.

questions.question: Occupancy of 104% in a model is best described as:
options: A mathematically valid but impossible result
questions.explanation: Nothing broke in the maths; the business logic is violated. A check should flag it.

questions.question: The balance check fails by $12,400. What should you do?
options: Trace the links to find the broken connection
questions.explanation: Never plug. Find and fix the cause.

points: Distinguish formula errors, invalid inputs, missing data and unreasonable results.
Build TRUE/FALSE checks with a small tolerance.
Trace precedents and dependents to find the source.
Never plug a difference.
